item.content:encoded:
WRAPUP 1-IMF chief urges cooperation on AI and war risks, as US hails economic momentum Reuters | Updated: 16-10-2026 18:33 IST | Created: 16-10-2026 18:33 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The head of the IMF on Friday appealed to global leaders to cooperate in the face of multiple economic risks, including rapid advances in AI and a prolonged war in the Middle East, as Washington hailed what it sees as US-led economic momentum. Their contrasting views echoed throughout this year's annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok, as finance officials and central bankers from around the world took stock of a global economy rocked by high inflation and rising interest rates that have kept growth sluggish and increased inequality. The IMF on Tuesday slightly raised its global growth forecast to 3.1% in 2026, well below the historical average, as it flagged significant growth and financial stability risks from a potential ending of the AI investment boom, growing debt levels and the ongoing Middle East conflict. Absent the US-Israeli-led war against Iran and Tehran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz that triggered a massive global energy shock, the IMF has said it would have expected AI to have fueled much stronger growth. On Friday, IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva said the sheer speed of technological change added to the long list of challenges, including disruptions to the global trading system, high food and energy prices and lingering wars, all of which threatened to widen the gulf between advanced economies and the world's poor. Bond markets, she said, were clearly sensing the risks, with US, German and Japanese 10-year sovereign yields reaching their highest levels in decades. "The need of the hour is for urgent and practical international cooperation," Georgieva, the first IMF chief from an emerging market economy, said at a plenary session on Friday. She told a subsequent panel that she spent sleepless nights worrying about how to regulate AI and ensure that poorer countries weren't left behind by its breakneck-speed development. US Treasury Under Secretary Erin Browne, in a call with reporters, pushed back against those warnings, hailing record highs on the US stock market, strong US economic output and improvements in Japan's economy. "The IMF needs to take a more balanced approach to assessing the global economic outlook," she said, adding: "The global economy has demonstrated significant resilience with strong US growth helping to support broader economic and financial stability." She said that the Fund should give equal consideration to "opportunities for positive economic shocks, particularly those driven by American innovation and super intelligence, energy abundance, and productivity-enhancing reforms." US President Donald Trump's policies on tax, trade, energy and deregulation were paving the way for stronger investment, higher productivity and durable economic growth, she said. AI JITTERS HIT STOCKS Emerging market stocks have been volatile in recent weeks, roiled by expectations of higher US interest rates that have sent borrowing costs sharply higher. Major markets have also been hit by the growing concerns over the AI investment cycle. South Korean shares posted their biggest weekly fall in 18 years as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom, while Japan's stock market lost 5.4% over the week. Eli Remolona, governor of the Philippines' Bangko Sentral ng Pilipanas, said in an IMF panel discussion earlier in the week that he was concerned Asia had not learned the lessons of its destructive financial crisis in the late 1990s. Before the Asian financial crisis broke out in 1997, economies drew huge capital inflows that prompted the World Bank to describe it as the "East Asian miracle," Remolona said. "Investment poured into Asia, and then you had the crisis because it wasn't really a miracle. I think we have to remind ourselves about that. We have to guard against that kind of crisis," he said on Wednesday. "We have not really been making a lot of effort looking at that kind of crisis." Illustrating the vulnerability to sudden shifts, Indonesian stocks fell 11.6% on Friday, their steepest one-day fall in 28 years, after global index provider MSCI said the Indonesian market was no longer worthy of "emerging market" status. Officials at the IMF and World Bank this week said they are seeing elevated demand for grant and loan programs. IMF strategy chief Christian Mummsen said the IMF's low-interest lending to low-income countries had quadrupled since the COVID pandemic, and demand was expected to remain strong. About 60% of the IMF's financing since COVID had gone to low-income countries, he said. Developing countries are increasingly outspoken about their concerns. Barbados this week joined a group of countries calling for the creation of an international panel to address inequality, citing geopolitical tensions, climate change and rapid technological advances that could further divide wealthy and poorer nations.

item.title: Pakistani forces accused of surging menace as Baloch teacher’s body found day after detention
item.description: The body of a schoolteacher was recovered in Pasni, Balochistan, a day after he was taken away by Pakistani security forces in front of his family and moved to an undisclosed location, as reported by ...
item.content:encoded:
Pakistani forces accused of surging menace as Baloch teacher’s body found day after detention The body of a schoolteacher was recovered in Pasni, Balochistan, a day after he was taken away by Pakistani security forces in front of his family and moved to an undisclosed location, as reported by The Balochistan Post. ANI | Updated: 16-10-2026 14:22 IST | Created: 16-10-2026 14:22 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The body of a schoolteacher was recovered in Pasni, Balochistan, a day after he was taken away by Pakistani security forces in front of his family and moved to an undisclosed location, as reported by The Balochistan Post. According to The Balochistan Post, the deceased was identified as Parvez, who taught Arabic at Government High School Babbar Shor. He originally hailed from Pedarak in Kech district. His detention left his family without information about his whereabouts. His body was recovered the following day and handed over to his relatives. Pakistani authorities have yet to issue a public statement addressing the allegations surrounding his detention and death. The incident has renewed concerns over alleged enforced disappearances and custodial killings in Balochistan. Similar cases involving educators have emerged across the province this year. In August, the Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC) reported that Hathim Baloch, a teacher from Panjgur, was found dead weeks after he was allegedly abducted by state-backed armed groups from Washbood Main Bazaar. In January, the bodies of two men, including school teacher Ayaz Baloch, were discovered in Berith, Awaran district. Ayaz, a resident of Kolwah in Kech, had reportedly been detained by Pakistani forces in October 2025 and remained missing until his body was recovered. His family alleged that he was killed in custody. The BYC’s human rights assessment for January to June 2026 documented 507 alleged enforced disappearances across Balochistan, including 135 students, teachers and researchers. The organisation further alleged that 32 missing individuals were killed in custody before their bodies were abandoned at various locations, as highlighted by The Balochistan Post. The report also highlighted violence against prominent academic and literary figures. Brahui-language writer and researcher Professor Ghamkhwar Hayat was shot dead in Nushki on May 16, while Baloch researcher Balach Khalid was killed in Turbat, as reported by The Balochistan Post. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
China's central bank to further open up Chinese financial markets to foreigners China's central bank governor pledged to further open up the country's vast financial markets, saying yuan assets can meet the growing diversification needs of global investors. Reuters | Updated: 16-10-2026 14:22 IST | Created: 16-10-2026 14:22 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

China's central bank governor pledged to further open up the country's vast financial markets, saying yuan assets can meet the growing diversification needs of global investors. Pan Gongsheng noted rising geopolitical risks, profound changes in the global economic landscape and rapid advances in AI. "China’s steady economic growth, and rapid development of high-tech industries provide solid support for RMB assets," a People’s Bank of China (PBOC) statement quoted Pan as saying in a Thursday speech given on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The PBOC will continue to expand risk management tools to expedite investment and financing, according to the statement. China has stepped up efforts to open its capital markets and to promote yuan internationalization, at a time when US President Donald Trump's trade war and unpredictable foreign policies dent trust in dollar assets. Global financial markets have also become more turbulent as investors increasingly worry about whether companies embarking on massive investment in AI will manage to make sufficient earnings gains amid higher borrowing costs. Pan said the PBOC will promote broader global acceptance and use of yuan bonds as eligible collateral, strengthen cross-border financial infrastructure connectivity and support the development of offshore yuan markets.

item.title: India's digital infrastructure among world's 10 highly effective reforms: CareEdge
item.description: India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) has emerged as one of the world's 10 highly effective structural reforms, supported by the wide reach of Aadhaar, the scale of Unified Payments Interface ...
item.content:encoded:
India's digital infrastructure among world's 10 highly effective reforms: CareEdge India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) has emerged as one of the world's 10 highly effective structural reforms, supported by the wide reach of Aadhaar, the scale of Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions and the growing use of digital payments by businesses, according to a report by CareEdge Global Ratings. ANI | Updated: 16-10-2026 14:12 IST | Created: 16-10-2026 14:12 IST

Representative image (Photo/Reuters) . Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) has emerged as one of the world's 10 highly effective structural reforms, supported by the wide reach of Aadhaar, the scale of Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions and the growing use of digital payments by businesses, according to a report by CareEdge Global Ratings. According to the report, India's digital infrastructure has expanded access to digital services, reduced transaction costs and supported financial inclusion and economic formalisation. The report examined 43 reform cases across 38 countries and classified India's digital public infrastructure among the 10 highly effective reforms. India's Aadhaar system covers more than 1.3 billion people, accounting for approximately 95 per cent of the population. Meanwhile, UPI processes more than 13 billion transactions every month, reflecting the scale of the country's digital payments network. The report also highlighted the growing use of digital transactions among micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), which account for more than 85 per cent of their transactions. This indicates greater integration of businesses with the formal economy. Nitesh Jain, Chief Rating Officer, CareEdge Global Ratings said,"India’s DPI stands out because it addresses foundational gaps that have historically constrained the reach of the formal economy: dependence on cash, limited access to banking and formal credit, and inadequate infrastructure for delivering financial services and welfare benefits at scale. The significance of this reform lies in creating a common digital foundation that can serve multiple economic and administrative functions simultaneously.” The report identified institutional coordination and interoperability as important factors behind the success of digital public infrastructure. Collaboration among government agencies, regulators, banks, payment networks and fintech companies has helped support its development and use. Of the 43 reforms examined, 10 were classified as highly effective, nine as moderately effective, 15 as work in progress and nine as least effective. Europe and the Asia-Pacific region accounted for eight of the 10 highly effective cases, with four each. Other reforms identified as highly effective included tax digitalisation in Greece, Germany's debt brake, banking reforms in Cyprus and Project Repeal in the Philippines. The report emphasised that announcing reforms is not enough to deliver lasting results. Effective reforms require coherent policy design, proper sequencing, clear mandates, political commitment and stakeholder support. Their success ultimately depends on credible implementation and measurable improvements. It also highlighted the need for future reforms to address emerging challenges, including advances in artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure requirements, climate risks, critical technologies and supply chains. (ANI)
